title: Cross-phase KV handshake and priority strategy
content:
Context
-------
This note sketches a concrete design for coordinating work between the prefill and decode phases that: (1) minimizes tail latency for streaming decodes, (2) avoids blocking high-priority interactive streams behind large prefill batches, and (3) keeps KV cache utilization high without causing hot-shard contention.

Motivation
----------
We see three recurring pain points in production traces:
- Long-running prefill microbatches (large contexts) can monopolize GPU kernel slots and KV cache memory, delaying latency-sensitive decodes.
- Opportunistic batching increases throughput but loses control over stream-level priorities; a single large prefill can push lower-priority work ahead of a short interactive decode.
- KV cache sharding causes localized load spikes when many decodes need the same KV ranges (e.g., similar prompts or common prefixes).

Goals
-----
1) Explicitly handshake between prefill and decode so prefill can supply hints and decode can reserve slots when needed.
2) Provide a lightweight per-stream priority mechanism that survives microbatch formation.
3) Implement KV-prefetch/lease semantics to allow decode to request ownership of cached KV shards without full-lock blocking.
4) Ensure kernel selection is aware of phase overlap: prefer decode-optimized kernels when low-latency is required, fall back to throughput kernels for large background batches.

Design overview (high level)
---------------------------
Introduce a CrossPhase Handshake (CPH) protocol and a Ticketed Priority Queue (TPQ) that operate in the request router and the local worker scheduler. Key concepts:
- Phase Token: metadata attached to each request: {stream_id, priority, estimated_prefill_size, decode_budget_hint}.
- Ticket: a short-lived reservation assigned to a stream that grants a decode slot or KV lease for a target worker. Tickets can be pre-requested during prefill so decode can start immediately once prefill finishes.
- KV Lease: a soft ownership of a KV shard for a short time window (e.g., 50-200ms). Holding a lease gives decode low-latency access to cached KV entries and prevents eviction for the lease duration.
- Kernel Hint: scheduler-level hint from router telling worker whether to prefer low-latency or high-throughput kernel paths for the incoming microbatch.

Flow (example)
--------------
1) Router receives an incoming request with large context (prefill+decode or only decode). It assigns a Phase Token and evaluates priority.
2) Prefill phase begins. During tokenization/prefill scheduling the router can:
   - Pre-request a Ticket for the decode phase if estimated_prefill_size < threshold OR if request priority is high.
   - Request KV lease for predicted hot shards referenced by the prefill (best-effort: probabilistic prefetch).
3) Workers run prefill microbatch. If decode ticket exists, the worker marks the microbatch with an opaque ticket id and attempts to schedule decode work to the same or nearby worker (to reuse KV and reduce cross-worker transfer).
4) When prefill completes, decode starts immediately if a ticket/slot is reserved. If not, the request enters TPQ; ticket-less decodes can steal short prefill slots if they meet priority delta thresholds.

Ticketed Priority Queue (TPQ) details
------------------------------------
- TPQ sits per-worker and globally (via lightweight directory) and orders epochs by (priority_score, fair_age).
- A priority_score is computed from explicit request priority + decoder-urgency estimate (time_in_system, client-SLO).
- Tickets are single-use reservations: a ticket guarantees a decode worker slot for up to ticket_timeout_ms. If not used, the ticket is released.
- Workers expose a small decode fast-path pool (N slots) that honors tickets and kernel-hints. Non-ticket decodes go into the general microbatch queue.

KV lease semantics and eviction policy
------------------------------------
- KV shards are the unit of lease. A lease gives the holder a short non-exclusive right to cache-resident KV segments. Multiple workers may hold leases for the same shard (read-mostly), but the system tracks lease counts to avoid memory overcommit.
- Lease acquisition is optimistic: the requester receives a lease token even if the shard needs to be loaded from remote, but the token includes a state flag (HOT | LOADING | STALE).
- Eviction rules: prefer evicting shards with no active leases and low promoted_score. Promoted_score depends on access frequency and current ticket demand.
- Reclamation: prefill phases can indicate shards eligible for eviction earlier (e.g., large context windows that will not be reused).

Kernel selection and phase overlap
---------------------------------
- Each microbatch is annotated with kernel_hint: {latency_preferred, throughput_preferred, balanced}.
- Router synthesizes kernel_hint using priority and decode_budget_hint. High-priority tickets => latency_preferred; very large prefill background batches => throughput_preferred.
- Worker runtime supports dual kernel pipelines; a microbatch can be routed to the low-latency kernel by draining/from the fast-path pool. If the fast-path pool is empty, the scheduler decides whether to preempt a lower-priority throughput job (soft preemption) or queue.
- Soft preemption is implemented by: (1) pausing kernel work at prefill/decode phase boundaries (safe points), (2) snapshotting KV cache pointers, (3) re-queueing remaining tokens into a new microbatch. This avoids expensive preemption in the middle of a long kernel invocation.\nMicrobatching adjustments
------------------------
- Elastic microbatch windows: microbatch thresholds are dynamic based on observed ticket pressure. If many tickets are held and decode fast-path slots are nearing exhaustion, shrink prefill microbatch size for interactive requests to reduce tail latency.
- Prefix-aware batching: group prefill work by predicted KV shard residency to maximize local cache hits and minimize cross-machine transfers. Use a short (5–20ms) batch formation delay to align similar shards.

Stream prioritization mechanics (practical heuristics)
---------------------------------------------------
- Priority tiers: realtime (chat/LLM UI), interactive (API low-SLO), batch (background, bulk inference).
- A priority delta threshold determines when a decode can steal capacity from an ongoing prefill microbatch. Example rule: if decode.priority >= prefill.priority + 10 OR decode.age > 300ms, allow steal at next safe point.
- Ticket size negotiation: small decodes can request 1 decode slot; long decodes can request multiple contiguous slots but pay a soft fairness tax (lower scheduling weight for next window).

Instrumentation and metrics to track
----------------------------------
- Ticket hit rate: fraction of decodes that had an available ticket upon prefill completion.
- Average handshake time: time from ticket request to ticket assignment.
- KV lease miss rate and average shard load latency.
- Tail latency P95/P99 for realtime tier before/after enabling TPQ and tickets.
- Kernel path split: % microbatches using latency-optimized path vs throughput path.

Operational knobs
-----------------
- ticket_timeout_ms (default 150ms)\n- fast_path_pool_size per GPU (default 8)\n- lease_window_ms (default 200ms)\n- prefetch_threshold (prefill_size under which auto-ticketing triggers)\n- batch_formation_delay_ms (0-20ms)

Safety and fallbacks
-------------------
- If ticket directory partition is unavailable, fall back to best-effort per-worker FIFO and conservative batching (no steals).
- If KV lease service is degraded, remove lease flag and revert to read-through loads with a throttled concurrency limiter to avoid thundering herd.

Prototype plan
--------------
Phase 1 (2 weeks): implement ticket plumbing in router + per-worker TPQ and fast-path pool; enable simple ticketing rule: auto-ticket for requests with estimated_prefill_size < 1024 tokens OR priority == realtime. Measure ticket hit rate and impact on P95.
Phase 2 (3 weeks): add optimistic KV lease tokens and lease-aware eviction counters. Track KV hot-shard contention metric.
Phase 3 (2 weeks): integrate kernel hints and soft preemption at safe points; run A/B on interactive-heavy workload.

Experiments and success criteria
-------------------------------
- Run replayed traffic from two customers (one interactive chat app, one bulk scoring job). Target: reduce realtime P99 by >= 30% with < 5% throughput regression for batch workloads.
- Ticket hit rate target >= 75% for interactive streams at 95th percentile of load.

Open questions / trade-offs
-------------------------
- Lease granularity: shard vs segment vs token-range. Finer granularity reduces overfetch but increases metadata overhead.
- Ticket staleness and cross-region routing: is it worth creating multi-region ticket fallback logic? Complexity vs benefit for multi-tenant customers.
- Fairness: long-lived high-priority streams could starve throughput customers if tickets are abused. Consider token bucket or credit accounting per-customer.

Notes / TODOs
------------
- Add diagram showing ticket life-cycle and RPC flows (router -> ticket-directory -> worker).
- Simulate extreme hot-shard scenario with synthetic traces to tune lease_window_ms and eviction thresholds.
- Draft PR for router metadata changes (add Phase Token headers).

Closing
-------
This design trades modest added control-plane state (tickets, lease counts) for improved tail-latency guarantees and better KV cache locality. The handshake model keeps the router informed of upcoming decode demand and gives the runtime cheap primitives (tickets, leases) to prioritize time-sensitive streams without sacrificing throughput for background workloads.

Comments welcome — specifically: is ticket_timeout_ms too short? are we underestimating metadata costs for leases? any thoughts on simpler alternatives (e.g., strict preemption at microbatch boundaries without tickets)?

-- Aisha
